title: The M-G-M nostalgia theater jazz proposal
summary: Monk wrote a proposal for jazz in the M-G-M theater and monthly Sunday spectaculars after Bill DeAngeles asked for it on paper.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Managers, bookers and the business of getting work

blocks.x: And it looked like it was hitting the bottom for me again. I went out again, and I made a couple of breakthroughs, through the entertainment directors, at least to talk to them, a couple of them. But one that really was like the straw that broke the camel's back, I should say...At the M-G-M they were like new, they had just opened, sort of. And the first, at the grand opening, I was fortunate enough to work in the lounge with Mavis Rivers. Mavis Rivers was one of the opening acts in the lounge and she was there three or four weeks. And I was there with her and I had a chance to meet the entertainment director, Bill DeAngeles, at the time.

And after the engagement and everything, I made my way back to Bill DeAngeles and started talking to him about it. Because I felt the M-G-M was the ideal place. Here's a hotel, brand new, coming in with new policies, new concepts. They had jai alai, a whole new concept of gambling, that game, jai alai from Mexico. They had downstairs a theater where nostalgia movies were shown, through the old M-G-M archives, and all of that. And I was saying, 'That's the spot, because I know they're open minded about the subject. Not that jazz is new, but it's a concept that somebody should take advantage of.

And I was talking to Bill DeAngeles because I saw what I visualized was the theater downstairs. Nostalgia. Like the old days, we would see a movie and there was a stage performance. There's be a live...a stage thing. When I used to work with Lionel Hampton, when we traveled, we'd work the Fox Theater...Work the old -- what's the name? -- the Regal Theater. We worked the Apollo Theater, and that's what it was.

The Earle and, yeah, all those, we worked those, the Howard Theater in Washington. And when we worked in them, it was like, you run the movie and then you'd run the...The band would come out and play, dancers would be on, and so-and-so. Then run the movie and so-and-so. So I thought that was a great piece for nostalgia.

The room seated about 250-200, whatever. Why didn't they do that down there, against the movies, you know? On a consistent basis. And once a month, we would take the big room upstairs, the show room, and do a spectacular, bring in a concert on Sunday afternoon.
How did they feel about it?

Bill DeAngeles thought it was a great concept, and 'I think so-and-so.' And I sat in his office and talked with him. He said, 'The one thing you have to do is put this on paper. You have to bring me a proposal, so I can submit it to the board. I can't go over there and say, well, Monk's got a great idea, he thinks so-and-so. You got to give me a break-down of the cost and samples of who the artists---- and all this sort of thing.

See, I wasn't into that, but I could see what he was saying and I said, 'Hey, wait, I'll do it.' Because I felt like this was a winner. I came home and it must have taken me, even though I had it all in my head, I put in on paper, to write all of it out and get it down, and get it... I had this friend of mine type it up and put it in a nice beautiful folder. And ready to send it back that I got it all out of my head and on paper. And I went through it over and over, tore up pages and scratching out and... I had a project!
